narrationBlocks: What did Noah's ark actually look like? You probably picture a familiar wooden ship with a sloping roof and animals crowding the deck. But Genesis describes rooms, three levels, and coating inside and outside.

The story also includes provisions, birds, and a long wait for dry ground. Let's follow those details through the text with clearly attributed evidence, separating its descriptions from the choices an illustrator still has to make.
chapters.hookSentence: What did Noah's ark actually look like?

chapters.purpose: Chapter two ONLY: blueprint in Genesis 6:14-16. The text specifies rooms, three levels, side door, wood and pitch inside and out; it gives proportions, but do not convert cubits to a precise modern length. Distinguish stated instructions from the interpretive positions of rooms, roof shape and the drawn cutaway. KJV says window, Wikipedia records roof/skylight ambiguity: do not present one settled modern engineering diagram or identify an exact wood species. The familiar ship-and-sloping-roof picture belongs to interpretive illustration; if discussing a later historical depiction, attribute the specific source rather than asserting most pictures are wrong. Each paragraph adds a concrete distinct textual observation, not 300 words saying we do not know. narrationBlocks: Start with the passage that describes the construction. In Genesis, the instructions give the ark a length of three hundred cubits, a width of fifty, and a height of thirty. Those are proportions you can put beside a drawing. They are not a photograph, and they do not tell an illustrator exactly how to shape every piece of the hull. Our picture is a way of following the description, with the interpretive choices left visible. Now look through the side of that picture. The text specifies lower, second, and third stories. There are three levels to account for, even if a familiar illustration hides everything beneath a roof. Genesis also calls for rooms. The passage does not supply a numbered floor plan assigning a particular room to a particular occupant. So the partitions in this cutaway help explain the instruction; their exact positions are our illustration, rather than another sentence from the text.

Next, follow the surfaces of the wood. The instruction calls for pitch within and without. An explanation that shows only the outside coating misses that second surface. We can draw a small wooden section and show both faces without claiming to have recovered an actual piece of the vessel. The passage names wood for the construction, but reading that instruction is different from holding a verified construction sample. We will leave the timber species unidentified in the artwork. Finally, notice the opening and the door. The King James wording describes a window and places the door in the side. It does not give us a detailed drawing of either feature. Keep those explicit instructions separate from the roof, curve, fittings, and decorative details an artist chooses to add. The description gives us something concrete to inspect, while still leaving parts of the picture open.

chapters.purpose: Chapter three ONLY: occupants and provisions from Genesis 6:18-21 and 7:1-16. Noah’s household enters in the narrative, and the instruction includes gathering food. Distinguish the general two-of-each instruction in chapter six from chapter seven’s clean/unclean distinction. If mentioning the sevens, quote or accurately paraphrase the supplied KJV instead of silently converting it into a disputed exact count; do not claim every species had exactly one pair. No species totals, deck assignment, animal biology calculations, air conditioning, manure disposal machinery or invented crew tasks. Show illustrated examples, not a census claimed by the text. Keep this chapter about living occupants and provisions, not repeating the blueprint. EDITORIAL TEXT REPAIR: retain the TWO supplied narrationBlocks verbatim; they are reviewed original prose within this chapter’s existing word-budget range. Add source claims and visual descriptions without adding spoken words. Do not summarize, pad, change the target, or repeat another chapter.
narrationBlocks: A drawing of the outside can leave out another instruction: food. In Genesis six, Noah is told to gather food for himself and for the animals. That changes where we direct our attention. Instead of looking only at the outline of the vessel, imagine a supplied interior. Our illustration can include stored provisions, but their arrangement is an explanatory choice. The passage does not hand us an inventory of containers or a storage diagram for every room. The household matters too. The account names Noah, his wife, his sons, and his sons' wives as entering with him. These are occupants in a narrative, rather than passengers whose cabins we can identify from a surviving plan. A careful cutaway can make space for people and provisions without pretending the source specifies exactly where everyone slept. The interesting question is how much of a familiar scene comes from those instructions, and how much we add when we turn words into a picture.

The animals introduce a detail that a single line of pairs can conceal. Chapter six gives the general instruction about two of every sort. Chapter seven then distinguishes clean beasts from beasts that are not clean. In the King James wording, the former are taken by sevens, the male and his female; the latter by two, the male and his female. Those instructions should not disappear behind the simplified claim that every animal group had exactly one pair. Nor do we need to turn this passage into an invented total of modern species. We can show the distinction as a labeled illustration, keeping the wording tied to its passage. The account goes on to describe the entry into the ark and says that the Lord shut Noah in. That is how Genesis tells the event. It does not give our illustrator a closeup diagram of the door mechanism.

chapters.purpose: Chapter four ONLY: the long wait in Genesis 7-8. Begin with the source-grounded raven/dove tests, then explain why the rain, prevailing water, grounding, dry ground and permission to leave are different narrative milestones. In Genesis 8 the dove first finds no rest, later brings a freshly plucked olive leaf, and at the later sending does not return. Do not confuse the raven with the dove or turn the dove’s absence into archaeological evidence. If mentioning duration, distinguish forty days/nights of rain from the water prevailing a hundred and fifty days; avoid building a complete arithmetic calendar or exact historical date. Mountains of Ararat in the text do not identify a verified wreck on a modern peak. Attribute events to the biblical narrative. No repeated construction explanation. Add source claims and visual descriptions without adding spoken words. Do not summarize, pad, change the target, or repeat another chapter.
narrationBlocks: The story has a surprisingly concrete way of describing the wait: it follows birds going out from the ark. In Genesis eight, Noah first sends a raven, which goes to and fro. He also sends a dove to see whether the waters have abated from the ground. On that first journey, the dove finds no resting place and returns. Noah reaches out, takes it, and brings it back inside. A later sending gives the reader a different image. The dove returns in the evening with an olive leaf in its beak. Then, after another wait, Noah sends it out again, and this time it does not return. Keep the birds and their actions separate. The raven is not the bird carrying that leaf. These are details of the account, useful for following its sequence; they are not a photograph or a recovered object identifying the location of a wreck.

Now step back from those flights and look at the larger sequence. Genesis says that rain falls for forty days and forty nights. It also speaks of the waters prevailing for a hundred and fifty days. That is not a statement that rain kept falling for all those days, and we should not simply add the periods together as though the text had given us two consecutive modern stopwatch readings. The water rising, the ark coming to rest, the ground becoming dry, and the instruction to leave are different moments in the narrative. A picture that jumps straight from the first rain to animals walking outside can compress that extended wait into a single scene. Our timeline keeps the moments distinct without assigning the story an independently verified historical date. When the account places the ark on mountains, that description belongs to the text. It does not establish that a particular object photographed on a modern mountainside is the vessel.

chapters.purpose: Resolve the episode’s core question: a drawing can follow explicit textual details while still making interpretive visual choices. Introduce the narrative’s exit/altar in Genesis 8 and covenant/sign of the bow in Genesis 9 as the story’s own conclusion, attributed respectfully to the text; no proof/disproof or invented narrator motives. Explain why source-reading and an archaeological recovery are different claims, without introducing alleged discoveries. A single concise callback to the three levels suffices; do not repeat whole earlier claims/sentences. narrationBlocks: When the instruction to leave finally comes, Genesis describes Noah going out with his household and the animals. The story then turns to an altar that Noah builds. Those details belong to the account's movement beyond the enclosure of the ark. They do not tell us the vessel's final archaeological history, or authorize an illustration to fill in an excavated wreck. In the following chapter, the narrative describes a covenant and the bow in the clouds as its sign. That is the story's own conclusion, which we can explain respectfully without presenting an illustration as evidence that every depicted event has been independently reconstructed.

Return to the drawing we started with. We can now identify which features came from particular lines: rooms, levels, an opening, a side door, provisions, and coating on both surfaces. Other features remain choices made to create a readable picture. There is a useful difference between saying that a drawing follows the passage and saying that it shows the exact appearance of an object recovered by archaeology. Our reconstruction is doing the first. That distinction lets the text supply the details it actually contains, while keeping the artwork honest about the gaps it fills.

narrationBlocks: Before you move on, try looking at an ark illustration without starting with its most dramatic feature. Look past the animals on the deck. Look inside the structure, then follow the door and the coated surfaces. Ask which part of the image you could point to in the passage, and which part makes the scene easier to imagine. You do not have to reject an illustration to notice that distinction.

It is the same habit we use when comparing familiar pictures of biblical angels with the descriptions in their passages. The image can catch your attention; the next step is to read the source beside it. If that contrast interests you, our angels episode follows those differences in more detail. For this ark, keep one question with you: what did the text give the artist, and what did the artist supply?

factualCorrections: Do not present a single common illustration as the exact appearance of the ark.
Three levels are stated, but the location/size of individual drawn compartments is an interpretation.
The general two-of-each wording does not erase the additional clean/unclean instructions in Genesis 7.
A hundred and fifty days of prevailing water is not a hundred and fifty days of rain.
The olive leaf is brought by the dove, not the raven.
Mountains of Ararat in the narrative do not confirm any modern wreck or exact archaeological location.
Any later roof, skylight or wood discussion must follow the actual retrieved wording and acknowledge interpretation.
